transcript: Hey, welcome to Socialism for All. This file's being recorded for the September2024 edition of Socialism for All. And this quick video is an introduction toour anti-Trotskyism playlists. If you like this video, please click like andsubscribe and consider supporting on Patreon or buy me a coffee atpatreon.com/socialismforall or buymeacoffee.com/socialismforall.There are links to Patreon and buymeacoffee in the video description.So, Trotsky's defenders often try to portray him as the best Bolshevik whoever was, the true adherent of Leninism, and the rightful leader of the partyafter Lenin's death, a position which was unjustly usurped by the evil Stalin,who then led the revolution into ruin. While many Trotskyists will admit thatTrotsky and Lenin had differences over the years, they tend to downplay themsignificantly. However, they were in fact fundamental, and they never reallyceased. The reality is that Trotsky only joined the Bolsheviks a few monthsbefore the 1917 revolution. And for about 15 years prior, he fought them andcollaborated with anti-Bolshevik trends, which had they been more successful,might have crushed the possibility of revolution and the subsequent foundingof the USSR. Lenin responded with many brutal criticisms of Trotsky acrossdozens of works, even after Trotsky became a Bolshevik. Some of the moresalient of which we will be recording and entering into the Lenin againstTrotsky video playlist, which already exists on the channel. We also havebegun a more general anti-Trotskyism playlist, which will feature a few ofthe Lenin against Trotsky texts, but will focus more on third-party workswhich criticize Trotskyism and its legacy. This video is intended as abrief background on Trotsky, and it'll be included at the top of both videoplaylists. So, Trotsky was an intelligent person,and there are some attractive qualities to his writings, which have helped towin him followers. He also made significant contributions to the 1917revolution and civil war as leader of the Red Army. However, reviewingTrotsky's history of ideological positions and struggle, it makes senseboth that Stalin rather than Trotsky found his way to the top of theBolshevik leadership and that the tendencies Trotsky representedultimately would be combated formally by the Soviet government. The followingcursory outline of Trotsky's history with the Russian Social Democratic LaborParty or RSDLP was adapted from Francisco Martins Rodriguez's Trotskybefore 1917. In 1903, when the party was strugglingto define itself and its role toward the revolutionary masses, Trotsky took aMenshevik line by siding against many of the positions which Lenin had taken inworks such as 1902's What Is to Be Done? In the following years, including the1905 revolution, Trotsky tried to sidestep the debate that was raging inthe party about alliances to the peasantry or the liberals by advancinghis own theory of permanent revolution. In practice, he would advance a linethat in some ways would agree with Lenin while remaining grounded in Menshevism.Following the 1905 revolution, as was often the case, Trotsky formed his owngroup which attempted to straddle the line of struggle between the Mensheviksand Bolsheviks despite Lenin's insistence that unity between Marxists,Bolsheviks, and opponents and distorters of Marxism, Menshevik liquidators, wasnot what he sought. Although Lenin attempted to work with Trotsky duringthis time, he would eventually accuse Trotsky of favoring the Menshevikopportunists and break it off. Following this in the early 1910s, Trotskycollaborated with the liquidators against the Bolsheviks. And when theliquidators formed their own party in 1912, the RSDLP(M), Trotsky continuedhis hopeless and harmful {quote} independent conciliation efforts whichled him to work alongside some of the fiercest anti-Bolshevik opportunists.This was a trend with Trotsky of which criticism from Lenin can be seen inworks such as 1914's disruption of unity under cover of outcries for unity. AsWorld War I was launched by the imperialists and the Bolsheviks busiedthemselves with vigorously attacking Kautsky and the other opportunistleadership of the Second International, which had endorsed the war at a timewhen they should have been making preparations to take advantage of thisemerging revolutionary moment. Trotsky in some ways appeared to support theanti-war, pro-revolution movement, but refused to cut ties with the Kautskyitesand muddied the revolutionary messaging so badly that Lenin accused him inpieces such as the defeat of one's own government in the imperialist war in1915 of using {quote} high-flown phraseology to justify opportunismworthy only of {quote} conscious partisans or helpless satellites of thesocial chauvinists. Lenin considered Trotsky to be in the latter group,basically lumping him in with Kautsky. When Trotsky finally joined theBolsheviks and settled in the post-1922 period into the Soviet government, hisvacillations were well-known and can be understood as a continuation of his twodecades history of appearing to take on some Leninist positions while remaininggrounded in Menshevism and conciliationism and fighting Leninism inpractice. Although Trotskyists will cite a 1917 quote from Lenin of dubiousorigin about there being {quote} no better Bolshevik, the mountain ofLenin's writings against Trotsky, as well as Trotsky's actual stances inhistory, tell a different and much clearer story about why thisanti-Bolshevik figure never found his place in the party he so long hadfought. Following Trotsky today, as so many parties in the US and UK have donewhile claiming to be the real Leninists, Bolshevik Leninists, etc., is simplywrong.
